utterances.text: Your Honour, we can call the witness Schouten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that may be so; he can explain it. But there are so many problems. There is a very, very well-known cause in Australia where somebody was convicted on the basis of what was said to be a positive reaction to blood. It was under the dashboard of a car and it was alleged that a baby had been murdered in the car. When the matter was reopened, it was found that it was some type of adhesive that had proved positive. And this expression "positive" is absolutely meaningless unless we can have an expert here to tell us what is meant. And so far as I'm concerned, we have no indication before us at the moment upon which we can rely to establish that there was anything to do with blood there at all. The fact that it was not established does not mean that there was no blood there, but you have no evidence at the moment upon which any Trial Chamber could rely to say that the testing showed that there was blood there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I totally agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Well, then we can forget the rest of this cross-examination along this line, I think. Mr. Bakrac, let's get on to your next point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It is quite enough. Now I should like to ask the usher to show photograph 407474, and 407475, the bottom photograph, the lower photograph first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Manas, will you please show -- point to us the windows of Room 17 in the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, the witness is indicating the fourth window from the left and also the fourth window from the right on the first floor of the administrative building, that is, the floor above the ground floor; and at the end of the photograph of that floor is marked 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'd agree with you that it is the fourth window from the right. I'm not altogether certain it's the fourth window from the left. But it's sufficient, is it not: The fourth window from the right is the one to which the witness was pointing? The photograph has not been a complete one. We don't know. Oh, I see. It's moved now. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or maybe, Your Honours, the third window from number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. That might be the best. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can the usher please help to show the witness first photograph 407529 and then 407528.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Ms. Manas, can you agree with me that this photograph was taken from the bank opposite from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the opposite side of the river bank but on ground level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you. Now will you please tell me: What can you see from here, I mean part of the KP Dom compound?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you be quite specific to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you agree that on the other side of the bank you can see the penitentiary, the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And that in front we see the building which we call the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That above the administrative building and behind it we can see a small part of the prisoners' quarters?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you also see some windows in that part below the roof?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which room that is?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That will be the right wing of the prison quarters, third floor, Room 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many windows can you see?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now will you please look at the second photograph on that same sheet, the upper one. You already commented on this photograph, but here I should like to ask you to explain to us for the record what you told us, that this photograph was taken from Room 23. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you then please explain to us what does this yellow arrow point at?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The yellow arrow indicates what I can see from Room 23, the bridge, that part of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The Defence needed much more precise information for the record. You tell us part of the bridge, but part of the bridge could also be the road. What part -- or fence or whatever. So can we agree that you actually see the upper part of the metal structure of the bridge arch, and a very, very small part of this arch?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Will you then please tell us for the record what is, in your view - I don't know if you measured it. Perhaps you did, perhaps you didn't - how high is that arch, or rather what is the span between the base of the bridge and the upper part of the arch?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't work on the bridge, didn't take any measurements from the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But roughly could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke to us about Room 17 and some marks, graffiti on doors showing the BiH coat of arms and letters B-I-H, and also similar inscription on a metal cupboard. Now, in your investigative work, did you find that before the 18th of April there were Green Berets who stayed in the KP Dom for a while?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a period of one month.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would you then grant that it might be possible that they left behind those graffiti, those inscriptions, when they left?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You told us also that, on the walls of isolation cells, you found some inscriptions which you cannot remember right now and that you photographed, but why didn't you write down what they said; or when the photographs could not be taken, why didn't you try to photograph them again?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very faint. From whatever the interpreter could read and figure out, those are the words which are found very emotional.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Doesn't it sound logical to you that the prisoner would write something like that, and that it will then stay behind him whilst, of course, the guards could see that, and then punish that same person again for writing it?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question is, Ms. Manas, did you do any other investigative work in the KP Dom which you did not mention to the Court today? Did you try to establish how this sound propagates? Did you make some experiments with throwing objects from the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean, "throwing objects from the bridge."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you do any acoustic measurements? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps throw some sacks off the bridge across from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't equipped with sacks, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So just nothing, you did not try to throw anything from the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you measure the distance between the main entrance into the KP Dom to the bridge on the Drina?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, on a few matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, to start with, actually the end of your answers to my colleague, he asked you if you established during your investigation that Green Berets stayed or had taken over the KP Dom for some time. First of all, who are the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Green Berets were the, from my investigation, they were the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you actually find out that they stayed there, or is it what Mr. Rasevic told you?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's what Mr. Rasevic told me, only know that the Muslim forces occupied the KP Dom from the beginning of April to the beginning of May, but I don't know which particular unit or military unit or paramilitary unit occupied the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you have also here seen this view, this photo with the view of room -- from Room 23 onto the bridge over the Drina. When you made this photo, were you just standing normally on the ground -- on the floor of this room, or were you on a higher level? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the room itself, no, I wasn't standing on the ground level. The only way I could see the part of the bridge was I stood on a heating device in the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment. Are you going to pursue that line, or have you finished with that particular subject?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but if you have another question ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that the photograph must have been taken from a window which was not one of the three windows you could see from the photograph taken on the other side at ground level. If you had been standing at one of those windows, you would have had no difficulty seeing the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We better sort out just from which part of Room 23 the photograph taken out from the room was taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Room 23 would be through the trees. The arrow that's pointing to it on the photograph itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I think we put the photo on again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: My understanding was that the challenge to the Prosecution evidence related to the witness who was on the floor below who said he could see the bridge from his room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. But it may as well be that the witness is mistaken about the room number; therefore, I think we should clarify with Ms. Manas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you please look at the two photos in front of you, and first on the top photo, can you tell us the year and number?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did I understand you correctly, when you made this photo, you were standing on the heating?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stood on a heater because this is the only way I could see something that was -- the bridge itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. And can we have a look on the photo below. That would be then the photo - which number is it? I can't see - 7529. Which of the windows would it be, the windows that we can see overlooking, overlooking the administration building?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the last floor, so it will be the third floor of the right wing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is not actually the three -- there are three -- is it correct that there are three windows overlooking the administration building in clear view?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here from the photo, yes, there's three windows.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And they are not actually in the middle -- they're not at the end, they are not at the end of the building?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So where would you have been?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have been there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness was pointing behind the trees.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: 'Cause that's where you would find Room 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us from that photograph which room those three windows belonged to? Don't guess. I mean, if you can really tell us.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, I didn't go through all the rooms. I only went to Room 23 to see if I could see the bridge from that window 'cause I didn't see the bridge from the window itself, and I found a position where I could observe the bridge. It was on a heater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But it wasn't from any of those three windows that you can see on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That makes sense of it, then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I think that clarifies it, really. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I have one more point. Mr. Bakrac asked you about what Mr. Sekulovic told you about the guards and to which ministry -- by which ministries they were supervised, and I would like to read something that you put in your report, that is the Exhibit 41, the Prosecution Exhibit 41, and on page 5 it says: "The guards employed by the Ministry of Justice worked on both parts of the prison. The question how the guards regarding the military section would be supervised and by whom he did not answer. He only mentioned that while Krnojelac was in charge, he had to coordinate with a certain deputy, Marko Arsovic." Is that what you recall about the conversation, or is it even in your notes?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you're reading that from my notes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you, as you have your notes with you, could you please double-check the name Marko Arsovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Because, Your Honour, I just checked the list of employees, that is P3, and there is no Marko Arsovic on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So I wonder, Ms. Manas, could you check your notebook, your investigator's notebook, if you can find that name in there, or if it is a mistake, maybe.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's a name that I got at that time. No, it's not in my notebook, so it could be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the name "Marko Kovac"? Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kovac would seem more likely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I heard of that one taking witness testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did you hear about Marko Kovac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. This name reminds me more of something, I don't know what. The first name is the same, and these are two completely different surnames. I really don't understand the purpose of the question. Arsovic and Kovac, I don't know what does it remind the witness of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you are trespassing not only upon leading questions, but you are going well beyond anything that arises in cross-examination. If you want leave to investigate in-chief with this witness about this name, by all means. I'm not sure the way you're going about it would be permissible, but you may certainly try to clean up if there is an error made.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I thought that the witness would have her notebook and we could check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It does not have a name, unfortunately, so I think that line of inquiry is probably dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But I wouldn't stop you if you do it as part of your evidence-in-chief, and then it could be cross-examined upon, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you want to do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The problem is that this name -- I've never heard this name before, not from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, but the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness has mentioned it, but I think it may be a mistake. But we cannot clarify it, that's now clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We can only accept that she was told that name by Mr. Sekulovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sekulovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Sekulovic. So that's what she says. If you want to prove something different, I think you have to go to the fact rather than what this witness was told, 'cause she may not have been told the truth, or she may have been misled about something.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It doesn't really prove very much. That's what we're trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We're not pursuing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I'm actually through with my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may. I believe I'm entitled, just for the record, to clarify this matter. When the witness said that she could see the bridge only when she climbed the heater, she said it was the only place from which she could see the bridge. Now, what does "see the bridge" mean? It's very vague. What part of the bridge? Which part of the bridge, or the whole bridge, or is it the part of the bridge that we showed, that is, this metal structure, this metal arch. It's simply vague. When she says "bridge," we simply do not understand. What does she mean; the whole bridge, or a part of the bridge, and which part of the bridge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What do you say about there being some uncertainty is correct. The question which was asked was an appropriate one in re-examination. The Prosecution hasn't sought to work it out; therefore, it's the Prosecution that must suffer as a result of it. My understanding is, and it seemed to be very clear from the photographs, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- the bridge could be seen from three rooms. That photograph that shows just the top of the bridge that you were asking her about, she says was taken further along from behind the trees. And when she went along there, the only way she could see the bridge was by climbing up on the heater. Now, that seems to be very clear. Nothing that she has said suggests that you could not see the bridge from those three rooms that you can see in the photograph. That's where the evidence lies, so far as I'm concerned, and the Prosecution hasn't sought to take it any further, which means you can take whatever advantage you can of that, but I don't see that you can now cross-examine further.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you're happy to leave it there, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It may well be clear enough, but you're happy to leave it there?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Thank you very much indeed. You may leave now, and thank you for giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is identified as 119, but there are no protective measures in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, could I ask the audiovisual director to turn the light off on the ELMO so there's no glare. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I notice that, according to the summary, he's going to talk about the beginning of the conflict. I think we've indicated we've really had enough about that, unless there's something really -- something new that this witness can tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This witness lived in the village Brod and he was part of an organised Territorial Defence. We would need to go into not a whole lot of detail but some explanation of it, in case the Defence wants to argue that he's a combatant. So there may be some issue there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. Yes. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Neither of those microphones are turned on. Would you please make the solemn declaration, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Ahmet Hadzimusic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What year were you born?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I was born on 11th of October, 1945.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I was born in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: My ethnicity is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: In 1992, could you tell us what you did for a living?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I worked in Maglic as a telephone operator.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How long had you been doing that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I worked for 27 years in that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Sir, I notice that when you came into the courtroom today you were using crutches. Do you have a physical disability?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was born in 1945, and in 1947 I contracted polio, and I've been using crutches ever since 1949.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you do your compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No, I did not do my compulsory military service. I went to the military office and I was issued a certificate certifying that I was unable to do military service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: That was because of your physical condition; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, due to my leg.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: In April of 1992, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I lived three and a half kilometres away, along the Drina River, in a place called Brod, at the foot of selo Dzidzevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you say "three and a half kilometres away," you mean away from what, or where?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: From Foca, from the town of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who lived there with you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I lived with my wife and three children.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you tell us, sir, how big Brod is?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Brod is a town, and there was also a factory Maglic, and it was an average-sized settlement. I don't know how to describe it. It was a small settlement, village. And the enterprise, the factory, was huge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was Brod an ethically-mixed town?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The part of the town that you lived in, was that mixed or was it predominantly one ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: The neighbourhood where I lived, around the bridge over Drina, was purely Muslim, and this village of Dzidzevo was mixed. It was approximately half, half.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Sir, when did the war in Foca start?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: The war in Foca started on the 8th of April, 1992, although there was some shooting prior to that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did the start of the war in Foca have an effect on those of you living in Brod?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Not a great effect; a slight one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did people living in Brod fear that the war might come to your town?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: They did. Yes, they did, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did the residents do anything about it, organise any sort of defence?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, there was, but an insignificant defence, because there were no weapons, so they couldn't really organise a defence, a serious one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did all the residents of Brod fear an attack on the town or was it a specific ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think that Serbs did not have fear, whereas we Muslims, we certainly did, because JNA helped the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did the Muslims in Brod organise a Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: They did in a small degree, because there were only a few of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How many people were participants in the Territorial Defence in Brod?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: In my village where I live, about 40 people, around 40.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you also participate?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did the participants of the Territorial Defence have weapons?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: We did, but very few.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: We had two machine-guns and a bit of -- several Thompsons; and those who were in the reserve police, they also had Kalashnikovs. There were two or three members of the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you have weapons, you personally?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I did, but not for a long time. I did not have it for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What was your role in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I was a sort of courier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did the Serbs living in Brod also arm themselves; could you see?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw it if they were shooting, which indicated that they had a lot of weapons and a lot of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When the war in Foca started, did you stay in your home or did you move someplace?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I stayed at home until April 20th -- actually, until April 18th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What happened on April 18th?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: On the 18th, they -- the buses from Montenegro started coming in. There was a lot of shooting going on, so I was afraid because of my wife and children, so I went up to the village of Dzidzevo and stayed with my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When did the attack on your village occur?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: On April 20th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Now, just prior to that attack, were there demands made for the people of your village to surrender?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know what the demands were?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: They asked us to surrender, to surrender our weapons, and to obey Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. their authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you say "their authorities," whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know which body was making this demand that you surrender your weapons and obey the authorities?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Across from the Drina River in Brod, there was a teacher called Krunic, Drago; Rangelov, Stamen; two brothers with the last name of Pijevic. I think that there was a Crisis Staff there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And was it the Crisis Staff that made this demand for surrender?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did your village surrender under the demand?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't. We did not respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: On the 20th of April, 1992, when did the attack occur?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: The attack occurred around 9.00 or 10.00, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was that in the morning or the evening?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: In the morning. Yes, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Just before the attack, where were you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I was staying at my friend's house in Dzidzevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you go outside?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Sometime around 8.00, I went out and I started walking down towards my house, towards my brother's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Why were you walking there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I went to inform him of the situation, because he was the chief one in the defence issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you see -- what were you going to warn him about? Did you see or hear anything?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I did not observe anything at the time. I did not hear anything at the time. Just for the sake of informing him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: On your way to your brother's house, did you see anything?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I did. I did see something. I did see soldiers, Chetniks, who surrounded these villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you able to see them with your -- just with your eyes or did you use anything?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I used binoculars, but they were at such a close distance that I could see them plainly with my eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What were the soldiers doing when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: They were marching soldier to soldier, shoulder to shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What did you do when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I turned back and started walking back to where my wife and children were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I had a revolver and I hid it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Where did you hide it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I hid it in the forest, along the road, below a road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I did it because I saw that it was all over, and I was hoping that the fact that I had crutches would save me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you say, "it was all over," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw a lot of troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And what was over?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: We were surrounded, and I could tell that the village would fall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What did you do after you hid your weapon?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I had a 5-litre jug, so I started walking towards my neighbour, and I was going to say that I went to fetch some milk.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did anything happen to you on the way?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No, nothing particular. Just Pero Elez, whom I knew from before, he stopped me and threatened me. He asked me where my brother was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was Pero Elez in uniform or civilian clothes when he stopped you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: In uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was he alone or with other people?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: He was not alone. There were a number of people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What kind of people?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know those people. Perhaps I was simply very much afraid, but there were a lot of people there, a lot of combatants, a lot of Chetniks there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were they dressed in uniform also?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: In -- there were people in, in JNA uniforms; there were people in blue uniforms, which I guess were some kind of work uniforms; there were also people in camouflage uniforms. Pero Elez was in one, and he had a kind of a white scarf. I remember that distinctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were Pero Elez and these other people armed when he stopped you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What did Pero Elez ask you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: He asked me where my brother was, and he told me to go and look for him so that he could surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Would you say that Pero Elez and all these other people with him, were they part of the attack, the attacking soldiers that you saw?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was the composition of those soldiers or those troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What did you do or say in response to Pero Elez?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I told them that I could not go and look for my brother, and that I also did not know where he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Then as the soldiers were proceeding, they were putting all the men together in one spot where there used to be a barn belonging to the cooperative.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you say "all the men," what men? You don't need to give us names, but what men are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Muslim; my people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you also taken to that barn?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What happened there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: From there, they took us to a field where they separated us because they had a list from which they were reading out and separating people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Whom did they separate out? And again, you don't need to give us their names, but how many and what was special about these people?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, they separated out about 15 or 20 people, and about the same number of us remained. We were ordered to sit down on the grass, and then we were ordered to lie on our stomachs and to graze grass, so that after that they again told us to sit up and to open our mouths and to show them whether we had any grass in our mouths, and if we had some, then we had to swallow it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did all the Muslim men have to do this?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did the soldiers say anything to you when you were ordered to do this? Were they making comments?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No, not a lot, but they did laugh.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Of the group of men that was separated out, were you part of that group?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I remained with the group that was sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What happened to the men who were separated out 'cause their name was on a list?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Ten or eleven of them were killed, and the remaining five or six were brought to KP Dom in the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How do you know that the men were killed?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, exhumation took place recently, and this is simply well known. I don't know how else to explain this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you of the group that showed up at KP Dom later, that the other men were killed?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was told this by my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What happened to you after that group was taken -- was separated out from you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: About 35 of us, I think there were that many of us, they made us walk down to the Drina bridge through the village. Then we crossed the bridge, and on the other side, on the opposite side next to Brod, it said in large letters, "This is Serbia." And then I walked another 50 or 80 metres, and there was a bus waiting for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You said "it" said, "This is Serbia." What was this written on?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: On the asphalt. On the lane, on the asphalt on the bridge, on the road of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did anyone -- did any of the soldiers make any sort of announcement when you were being taken over?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No, they said nothing. They merely fired, because there was a fountain to the right -- to the left, and to the right there were some shops, and there were very many troops there, and they simply fired rounds of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did Pero Elez say anything at that point?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Pero Elez, as we waited by the bus, he rode in a police car and used a PA device above the car: "We've done our bit. The village of Dzidzevo is in our hands."

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You said there was a bus waiting for you. Did you have to get on the bus?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. One by one, we got onto the bus. And there was a man with a piece of paper and a pencil. We would give him our name, and I said, "Ahmet Hadzimusic," and he would take it down, and after that, we were shown to our seats. And each one of us had to go through that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were people other than those from your village put on the bus?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No, only our villagers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: We were taken towards Foca, to the penitentiary, to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And when were you taken there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, now, I think it could have been 2 p.m. or perhaps 3.00 in the afternoon so that we arrived there around 4. I'm not quite sure. But nobody had a watch, so I wouldn't know the exact time, but I know that it was at about that time in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Where were you taken inside the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: They brought us to the KP Dom, and we then entered the administrative building through the main entrance, and in this hall there is a reception room left of the entrance. That is where we waited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you told why you were brought to KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody told us anything and nor did we comment. We only had to give our particulars at this reception desk again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did anybody make any comments about the fact that you walked with crutches?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, one of us, yes, one of us was a minor, a 16-year-old boy, and they -- somebody, one of them, said that that young man and I should go back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: One of them, who?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know his name, but the Chetnik. A Chetnik or a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you allowed to go home?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No. Afterwards, they asked me if I was Roko's brother, and I said yes, and the man said, "Oh, well, then, you have to stay."

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you interrogated that same day?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No. Well, yes, in the evening, around 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Where were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: We went through that corridor and entered the prison yard, and then we went up the stairs to Room 11. And in the anteroom where there is the lavatory, that is where they interrogated us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, again, those were men wearing JNA uniforms. There was a gentleman, well clean-shaved and all that, and he interrogated, and there were also others. And some were in civilian and some were in jackets, some were in uniforms, some were in gloves with the fingers cut off.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you interrogated alone or in a group of other men?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No, I was interrogated. There was my neighbour to my left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you tell us your neighbour's name?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Skender, Bajro.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Tell us please how the interrogation -- what it was like.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not asked anything. It was my neighbour who asked -- they asked him if he had -- they asked him about whether he was a member of the army, whether he had -- did he do his service, about me. And then they asked me if I knew what was an M-48, and I said I did not know what kind of a weapon it was. And then a man, a gentleman, and he had those huge eyes, and he had a knife, and he hit me on the head and said, "Don't you know Tandzara?" I said "I don't."

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you said "Tandzara," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, that Chetnik told me that that weapon was called M-48.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did anyone else hit you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Two behind and -- yes, on the back, and then when they took me to the area where the wash basins are, yes, that is where they took me, and there they beat me more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How did they beat you? On what part of your body and using what kind of instruments?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: On the back. They mostly hit me on the back, using either some batons or perhaps a hose of sorts, I don't know, because I was trying to make myself, to make myself smaller. I wasn't really looking what they were beating me with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What kind of injuries did you sustain?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I suffering from hernia because of these beatings, and my hands, too. I have an arrhythmia since, cardiac arrhythmia, sugar content in my blood is higher, my fingers get numb, and it all comes from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you beaten on your hands?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I must have tried to protect my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: With your hands?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was your neighbour also beaten at that time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No. Him, they beat later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Where were you taken after this?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: After that, they took us to isolation cells, all of us, all of us. They took all of us to isolation cells.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How many people were in the isolation cell with you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Fifteen there were in my isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How long were you kept in that cell?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Three or maybe four days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: With 15 of you in one of these cells, were you able to lie down to sleep?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No, we couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How did you sleep, then?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: While you were in the solitary cells, were you ever beaten?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I was not, but at night they came with torches and would search around our group. And my neighbour Ahmet Djuric I suppose could not look at that light, so the Chetnik hit him, and he was all blue in the face, as you could see in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you say "hit him," was he actually beaten, or how?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: He kicked him in the head.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you said you were able to see actually that his face was blue from that injury?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, yes, in the morning. In the morning when the day broke, then we could see -- then we could see a huge blister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I perhaps didn't understand it. What was the reason that he was kicked or hit?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, he kicked him because they would come at night and some of us they took out and beat; some they did not. But they would come with this big torches, and they would aim it directly into our eyes, and they would order us to look at that torch. And if somebody could not look at it, could not keep his eyes open or simply averted his eyes, then he would be hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who came at night? Again, you don't need to give us names, but what kind of people were they; soldiers, or guards, or civilians?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to say exactly, but they must have been -- they can't have been civilians. They must have been soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Why do you say --

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Very likely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Why do you say it was very likely they were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Because later on we were taken over by those who run the KP Dom before, those are -- the staff that worked there before the war, and they took us out of the isolation cells into rooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The incident regarding Ahmet Djuric is listed in [Realtime transcript read in error "^"] Schedule A, number 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not sure, though, that I understand his explanation as to why he thought they were not civilians. Perhaps you don't want to pursue it, but I don't understand it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you able to see what these people were wearing when they came into the solitary cell?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, they had uniforms and they had army trousers. I could see that. We were never allowed to lift our heads. They always ordered us to look down, so you tried to look on the sly. And you can see the army trousers. But they would wear some gloves with their fingers cut off and some jackets or -- what do you know, but we were not allowed to look.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you say the civilian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, excuse me, but -- I'm sorry to interrupt. I shall like to -- but in the transcript we do not have -- it says that this incident refers to -- and we do not see to what. I understood my learned friend, C27, but I see no link, so perhaps it would be good if we could clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... gave us the incident. The court reporters obviously missed it. They've just got the usual query, like an upside-down -- like a circumflex. What was it? 27?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: A7. Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you say the civilian authorities took over the prison and let you out, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Civilian authorities," I don't remember the witness saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He did -- he said that they were not civilians, the people who had been there before. Let me just see if I can find it in the transcript. I don't see any reference to him saying that of civilians. He said they were not civilians, the ones who had been there before. And then he said the ones who came to collect them were the ones who had worked in the prison before. That's what he may be referring to as civilians, but he didn't use the word.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I think I inserted the word on the assumption that he meant one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to explain that, sir. The people who let you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. out of the solitary cell, who were they?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Those people were those who had worked for the penitentiary before the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know if they were working there at the time you were brought in on the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Oh, no, I wouldn't know that. I wouldn't know that and couldn't, because I could not see, as those people forced us to look at the ground; they would not let us look.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know why you were let out of the solitary cells?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I don't, but they took us into rooms, from solitary cells into rooms, that is, rooms of the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you have contact again with the soldiers or the -- with soldiers while you were at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Before we move on to the rooms you were taken to: While you were in the solitary cells, you mentioned that, in addition to Mr. Djuric, that other people were beaten. Could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I can. When we came into the room - and I've heard that there was quite a lot of beatings had taken place there - my former neighbours, Kovacevic, Fikret Kovacevic, and Kemo Kajgana were not beaten, but Kovacevic was there, and they asked him, "What happens when you break three eggs?" And he said that you get cimbur. And then they cursed at him and used foul language, and they asked him again and then they beat him again. Then he said, "The sunny side up." And then they beat him once again, and then eventually he said that you got scrambled eggs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Which the word -- which his name "Kajgana" means.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: And after that, he was taken out of the solitary confinement, and then they said, "We did not call you. It was your neighbour who called you to come here. So here's a baton for you, and you go and beat him, because he called you." And then they thought that he wasn't beating him properly and then they demonstrated it on him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: This is very confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The interpreter was being very helpful to us there, but I think you had better sort that one out with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What she was saying was giving us the interpretation of the man's name, and that's probably right, but I think we better get it straight on the evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Let's just start with who was taken out of the solitary cell and beaten first.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: First they took out Kovacevic and beat him, and he was the one they asked those questions of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you actually see this or hear it, the beating?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I heard it. I could only hear it. I could not see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And they were asking -- the people who were beating him were asking him questions about different ways of preparing eggs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And the last answer that he gave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we still need -- I'm sorry to interrupt, but we still need to know what the significance of "cimbur" is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you answer that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I can. I can. "Cimbur" is our word for -- is our Muslim word for scrambled eggs, for scrambled eggs or an omelette, because that's that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And the second word he gave, maybe you can give us the word and then tell us what it means by describing it.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, this second one was an egg made sunny side up. That is, you don't scramble them; you just put them in the pan and you can see both the yolk and the white.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And finally, the third word that he gave.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: The third word, when he said what happens when you break three eggs, and then he eventually said, "Kajgana."

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And Kajgana is -- how can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, that is the last name of my neighbour's, Kemo Kajgana.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Kajgana" means scrambled eggs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And what happened then to Mr. Kajgana?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: And then Kajgana came and the selfsame gave the baton. He said, "We did not call you out, but he called you out. And since he called you out, let him beat you."

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who was asked to beat whom?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: When Kovacevic said, "Kajgana," and when he came, then those guards, or I don't know what they were, gave the baton to this one, to Kovacevic. No, no, no. Excuse me. They gave the baton to Kajgana and said, "You beat Kovacevic, because he's called you out."

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Kajgana did use the baton to beat Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was very gentle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And then did the people who were doing this, the ones you are not able to identify, what did they do or say?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: To Kemo or what? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: To either Mr. Kajgana or Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, since Kajgana did not really beat him properly, then they took the baton from him and demonstrated how one should beat, and so they beat him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: They beat Mr. Kajgana or Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Kajgana. They beat Kajgana to show him how he should beat, how he should deal those blows, and then they gave this baton to Kovacevic so that he would beat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Kovacevic then used the baton to beat Mr. Kajgana?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Correct. Yes, he had to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the beating of Mr. Kovacevic is listed in Schedule A at number 12, and of Mr. Kajgana at A, number 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Where were you when this was happening?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I was in the middle solitary cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you able to hear this happening?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, one is able to because it's not far away; it is the adjacent room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Now, when you were taken out of solitary, the solitary cell, what room were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I was taken to Room 13, the old part of the penitentiary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What other -- how long did you stay in Room 13?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: In Room 13, until early September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And what other rooms were you taken to during your time at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: From 13 I moved to 21. And do you want me to list all of them?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: From 21 I was transferred to Room 16; from 16 to 18; and from the 18, I went back to the old wing, to Room 14; and finally, I moved to Room 13; and from Room 13, I was transferred, on the 23rd of October, 1993, to the camp at Kula in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that it's 1.00. Perhaps we can take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you a different watch to mine?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: It's very hard to see from this angle. It looks approximately 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll let you off. Two-thirty, then, to resume. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.58 p.m. 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: While you were at KP Dom, were you ever interrogated again?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who interrogated you then?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I was interrogated by Zoran Vladicic, Tepavcevic, and the third one was named Vojo -- I have it written down. Would that be all right for me to check my notes?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I suppose you'd better confirm where the notes come from.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, we have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Are these notes that you yourself wrote?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Personally, myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When did you write them?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I wrote them when I received an invitation to come here and as I was preparing for my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: We have copies of these notes of the witness if the Court is interested. The Defence has a copy. I don't anticipate we'll be entering into evidence, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's the same evidence, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The same?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The one he wants to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to him referring to it, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You may proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Would it be the safer course of conduct, Your Honour, if we marked it for identification purposes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, it will be marked for identification. It will be marked for identification "5."

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I already mentioned the other two persons, and the third one was Vojo Starovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: During -- to the usher, it's not necessary to show the witness anything. He has his notes with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: During this interrogation, were you mistreated?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No. They did not mistreat me, but all three interrogated me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did they identify themselves as being part of the civil or military authorities?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No, they did not identify themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were they dressed in civilian clothes or in military clothes?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Other than the beatings that you described in or outside the solitary cells, were other detainees beaten?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd like for you to describe those for us, going in order of how they occurred. So to the best that you can remember, could you tell us who was beaten and when?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: On June 28th, which is Vidovdan, St. Vitus's Day, and prior to that day, Nurko Nisic who was a member of MUP of Foca, and he was beaten, and then he was taken back to the room. He was well beaten up. And on Vidovdan, on St. Vitus's Day, Nurko disappeared. He never again returned to the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You have identified Vidovdan as being the 28th of June. How many days before that was Nurko Nisic taken out and beaten?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Five or seven days prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know who beat him?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know at the time, but later on when I was freed, I found out that he was beaten by Zelenovic from Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I found that out from my distant relative who lived in this neighbourhood called Musala. He apparently boasted that he collected his debt from Nurko for everything that he owed him before that, but he did not kill him. He didn't want to kill him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who supposedly collected the debt?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You said "he" was boasting. Who was boasting this?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Zelenovic was boasting that, that in the old times when Nurko worked in the police, Nurko used to mistreat Zelenovic, and then later on when Zelenovic was beating Nurko, he apparently collected for this old debt. But he did not kill him; he let him live.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: While you were still in the KP Dom, did you -- well, when the beating was happening, did you actually hear it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I heard my neighbour and my close friend and relative, Kemo Tulek, because he was born in my neighbourhood and he was a member -- prior to the war, he was an employee of KP Dom, he worked in security, and I heard from him. I understood everything that he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you may have misunderstood my question. My question was about Nurko Nisic when he was being beaten. Can you tell us what he heard of that, before we move on to Mr. Tulek.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. Not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Nisic after he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I did see him when he came back from those main doors which lead -- which are in fact an entrance to the camp. He was wet and bloody and he was holding his stomach with one of his hands and he came back to room number 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you in room number 12 at that time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No. I was in Room 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How were you able to see him, then?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I saw him through the window, because we had the same entrance for the rooms 12 and 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was it daylight or nighttime?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Daylight. It was daytime, in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Nurko Nisic on Vidovdan, the 28th of June?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: He was taken away in the evening hours. They used to take people away between 5.00 and 10.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you say "used to," what was the time -- the period of time, I mean the dates? Between what date and what date are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you give us the date? Four or five days when?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, that was St. Vitus's Day, June 28th, and then a few days before that we were imprisoned, so we didn't really know what date it was and we lived in fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was it a few days before or a few days after St. Vitus's Day?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I think it was both before St. Vitus's Day, a day before St. Vitus's Day, and also afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Let's talk about St. Vitus's Day. Could you hear anything happening outside KP Dom on that day?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything particular, but there was a lot of shooting going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know why there was shooting?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: We found out later on that it was because it was St. Vitus's Day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was it a kind of celebration?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Just to clarify, is St. Vitus's Day a Serb holiday, a Muslim holiday, or ...

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: A Serbian holiday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What happened inside KP Dom on St. Vitus's Day?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: On St. Vitus's Day, people were taken away every evening for three or four days between the hours of 5.00 and 10.00 in the evening, around 5.30 or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Where were people taken?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: They were taken to the administrative building. Behind the reception area, there was a cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you actually see people being taken there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I could see them as they were being taken away, as they were walking along the path within the compound. We were able to see everything up until the main entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you able to identify the people who were taken there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, those that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were taken to the gate in this way during those few days you've described?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: About 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were they taken in groups or one by one?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: One by one. Babo and his son were the only ones that were taken away together.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What is Babo's real name?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Serif.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What is his last name?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I would have to look into my notes again, into my papers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: This is again the document which has been identified --

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I just remembered. Balic, Serif.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the people who were taken to the gate?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: They never came back to the camp. I don't know what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you hear the sounds of screaming, beating, or anything else after these people were taken to the gate?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Well, specifically, as far as my neighbour and childhood friend is concerned - I know his date of birth. His name is Kemal Tulek - I heard everything surrounding him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: I heard when he was taken away and I heard as they started beating him and when he pleaded with them, begging them in the name of everything that was sacred to him. And as he was pleading with them, they were cursing him, cursing his balija mother, his children.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you recognise his voice?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Where did Kemal Tulek work before the war?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: He worked in KP Dom. He was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honour, Kemal Tulek is listed in Schedule C at number 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And also, Serif Balic, who was mentioned, is in Schedule B at number 3, and his son is listed at Schedule B, number 4. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was anybody taken from your room?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: From my room, they took away Hamid Ramovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: He was taken after 10.00. He was not beaten there. He was taken -- he was driven elsewhere. We heard the car immediately after he left the room, and the car drove away. I think that he was taken away because he was not beaten there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you ever see Hamid Ramovic again after that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Hamid Ramovic is listed at Schedule C, number 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did any of the 50 people taken out to the gate in this way return? Did you see any of them?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: No, never. I inquired, but I never heard or saw any of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was a Salko Mandzo taken out to the gate as well?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
utterances.text: He was taken prior to these other people. He was also beaten, and then he was returned back to the room. And then they took away Mandzo Emir, a medical technician who worked in the Foca hospital. They in fact made a mistake, because both of them have the same last name, Mandzo, and they simply made an error when they took the first man out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How do you know that, that it was an error?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HADZIMUSIC
